{{Short description|American physicist (1934–2014)}}
'''Darrell Lynn Judge''' (November 2, 1934, [[Albion, Illinois]] – August 26, 2014, [[Temecula, California]])<ref name=obitDailyBreeze>{{cite news|title=Obituary. Darrell L. Judge|date=September 4, 2014|newspaper=Daily Breeze|url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/dailybreeze/name/darrell-judge-obituary?id=6818229}}</ref> was an American physicist, known for his research in [[solar physics]], [[spectroscopy]], and [[space science]].<ref name=obitUSC>{{cite news|author=Paisley, Laura|title=In memoriam: Darrell L. Judge, 79|date=August 29, 2014|website=USC News, University of Southern California|url=https://news.usc.edu/67829/in-memoriam-darrell-judge-79/|archive-date=August 16, 2022|access-date=October 6, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220816153212/https://news.usc.edu/67829/in-memoriam-darrell-judge-79/|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Biography==
His father was Virgil H. Judge, the first president of [[Lake Land College]] in [[Mattoon, Illinois]]. Darrell L. Judge graduated from [[Edwards County Community Unit School District 1|Edwards County High School]] in 1952. He received in 1956 a B.S. with a joint major in physics and mathematics from Eastern Illinois State College (renamed in 1957 [[Eastern Illinois University]]).<ref name=obitDailyBreeze/> At the [[University of Southern California]] (USC) he graduated in physics with an M.A. in 1963 and a Ph.D. in 1965. After receiving his Ph.D. he joined the USC faculty in the department of physics and astronomy.<ref name=obitUSC/> He became a full professor in 1975 and retired from USC in 2013 as professor emeritus.<ref name=obitDailyBreeze/> In 1978 he was the founding director of USC's Space Sciences Center (SSC) and continued as the SSC's director until his retirement in 2013.<ref name=obitUSC/> The present director of the SSC is Leonid Didkovsky.<ref>{{cite web|title=Space Sciences Center (SSC): Exploring the Solar System and Beyond|website=USC Dornsife College of Letters, Arts and Sciences|url=https://dornsife.usc.edu/space-sciences-center/main/}}</ref>

Judge did research on "space exploration, atomic and molecular physics, ultraviolet imaging, deep space and sounding rockets, and star systems."<ref name=obitUSC/> He and his colleagues designed and built various instruments used onboard NASA space flight missions. Such instruments were used to monitor electromagnetic radiation from the infrared to the extreme ultraviolet. The instruments were essential for experiments flown on the ''[[Pioneer 10]]'' and [[Pioneer 11|''11'']] space probes and the [[Solar and Heliospheric Observatory|SOHO (Solar and Heliospheric Observatory) spacecraft]].<ref name=obitUSC/><ref name=obitDailyBreeze/>

Darrell Judge received in 1974 the NASA Exceptional Scientific Achievement Award and in 1991 the von Humboldt U.S. Senior Scientist Award.<ref>{{cite web|title=Faculty Honors|website=Physics & Astronomy, University of Southern California|url=https://physics.usc.edu/Faculty/Prizes.html}}</ref>
He was elected in 1996 a fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] for "his pioneering work on the fundamental properties of atoms and molecules using selected [[Absorption spectroscopy|monochromatic photon excitation]] and [[Fluorescence spectroscopy|dispersed fluorescence]], and their applications in [[space physics]]."<ref>{{cite web|title=APS Fellow Archive|website=American Physical Society|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=1996&unit_id=&institution=University+of+Southern+California}} (search on year=1996 and institution=University of Southern California)</ref>

He married Marjorie Sanders Waddell in June 1959 in [[Brevard County, Florida]]. They met at [[Cape Canaveral]], where both were employed by the Ramo-Wooldridge Corporation (which became [[TRW Inc.]] in July 1965).<ref name=obitUSC/>

Upon his death, he was survived by his widow, two daughters, a son, and five grandchildren.<ref name=obitDailyBreeze/>
